subject: Polity
sub_topic: DPSP vs Fundamental Rights — conflict and reconciliation

concepts.name: Constitutional Hierarchy: Original Intent vs. Judicial Evolution
key_dimensions: Article 37: DPSPs are non-justiciable but fundamental to governance — precise legal meaning
Constituent Assembly debates: Ambedkar and Nehru's original vision of FRs vs DPSPs as complementary, not adversarial
The implicit superiority of Part III (FRs) over Part IV (DPSPs) in the original Constitution text
UPSC trap: 'Non-justiciable' does not mean 'unenforceable' — DPSPs can guide interpretation of laws

concepts.name: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) — The First Flashpoint
key_dimensions: Facts: Communal Government Order reserving seats in state medical colleges challenged under Article 15
Ruling: FRs prevail over DPSPs; Article 46 (promotion of weaker sections) cannot override Article 15(1)
Significance: First Supreme Court case to explicitly establish FR supremacy over DPSP
UPSC trap: This case directly triggered the First Constitutional Amendment (1951) adding Article 15(4)

concepts.name: First Constitutional Amendment (1951): Legislative Response to Champakam
key_dimensions: Addition of Article 15(4): Enabled special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, overriding Article 15(1)
Addition of the Ninth Schedule (Article 31-B): Protected certain land reform laws from FR challenges
Pattern established: Parliament amending FRs to accommodate DPSPs — a recurring constitutional strategy
UPSC trap: Article 15(4) was added, not Article 15(3) — Article 15(3) pre-existed for women

concepts.name: Property Rights Conflict: Articles 19(1)(f), 31 vs. Land Reform DPSPs
key_dimensions: Articles 39(b) and 39(c) vs. Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 — the central battlefield of the DPSP-FR conflict
A series of constitutional amendments (1st, 4th, 17th, 25th, 44th) progressively curtailed property rights to enable DPSPs
Article 31C (inserted by 25th Amendment 1971): Laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and (c) shielded from Articles 14, 19
UPSC trap: The right to property is now a constitutional right (Article 300A), not a fundamental right, after the 44th Amendment (1978)

concepts.name: Article 31C: Scope, Validity, and Judicial Scrutiny
key_dimensions: Original Article 31C (25th Amendment, 1971): Protected laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Upheld the original Article 31C but struck down the clause making a Parliamentary declaration non-justiciable
42nd Amendment (1976) attempt: Extended Article 31C to ALL DPSPs — struck down in Minerva Mills (1980)
UPSC trap: Post-Minerva Mills, Article 31C protects only Articles 39(b) and 39(c), NOT all DPSPs

concepts.name: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) — The Grand Reconciliation
key_dimensions: Established the Basic Structure Doctrine — both FRs and DPSPs are part of the constitutional conscience
Held that Parliament can amend FRs to implement DPSPs but cannot destroy the basic structure of the Constitution
Reconciliation formula: Harmony between Part III and Part IV; neither is absolutely superior to the other
UPSC trap: The case did NOT say DPSPs override FRs; it said Parliament has power to balance them within basic structure limits

concepts.name: Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) — Defining the Balance
key_dimensions: Struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs as violating the basic structure
Key principle: The balance between FRs (Part III) and DPSPs (Part IV) is itself a basic structure feature
Held that FRs and DPSPs are like two wheels of a chariot — destroying one destroys the Constitution's harmony
UPSC trap: Minerva Mills affirmed judicial review over constitutional amendments as a basic structure element

concepts.name: Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) — Ninth Schedule and Judicial Review
key_dimensions: Held: Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973 (Kesavananda date) are fully protected from FR challenge
Laws added to Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 can be challenged if they violate basic structure, including FRs
I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) reaffirmed and strengthened this position
UPSC trap: The Ninth Schedule does NOT provide absolute immunity — post-1973 additions are judicially reviewable

concepts.name: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) — Final Word on Ninth Schedule
key_dimensions: Nine-judge bench ruling: Laws added to Ninth Schedule after Kesavananda (1973) are open to challenge on basic structure grounds
FRs under Articles 14, 19, 21 are part of basic structure — laws abridging them cannot hide behind the Ninth Schedule
Significantly elevated the status of FRs relative to DPSPs in the property/reservation context
UPSC trap: The test is not 'which schedule' but 'does the law damage the basic structure including core FRs'

concepts.name: Judicial Interpretive Tool: Using DPSPs to Expand Fundamental Rights
key_dimensions: Courts use DPSPs to give substantive content to Article 21 — e.g., right to education (Article 45 DPSP → Article 21A FR)
Unni Krishnan v. State of AP (1993): Right to education derived from Article 21 read with Article 45 DPSP
Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985): Right to livelihood under Article 21 informed by Article 39(a) DPSP
UPSC trap: DPSPs cannot be directly enforced but can transform FRs — indirect enforceability through Article 21

concepts.name: Right to Education: DPSP to Fundamental Right Transition
key_dimensions: Article 45 originally: Free and compulsory education for children up to 14 years — a DPSP
86th Constitutional Amendment (2002): Article 21A inserted — free and compulsory education for 6-14 years as a FR
Article 45 DPSP simultaneously amended to focus on early childhood care for children below 6 years
UPSC trap: Article 21A covers 6-14 years; Article 45 DPSP now covers below 6 years — the age ranges differ and are often confused

concepts.name: Article 44 (Uniform Civil Code) vs. Articles 25–28 (Religious Freedom)
key_dimensions: Article 44 DPSP: Secure a Uniform Civil Code — a directive that directly tensions with religious personal laws protected under Article 25
Shah Bano case (1985): SC invoked Article 44 but Parliament reversed via Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986
Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) and John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003): SC repeatedly urged Parliament to enact UCC
UPSC trap: Article 25 allows regulation of secular activities associated with religion — this is the constitutional gateway for UCC

concepts.name: Article 39(b) & (c): Material Resources Distribution vs. Article 19(1)(g)
key_dimensions: Article 39(b): Distribution of material resources of community for common good — enables nationalization laws
Article 39(c): Prevents concentration of wealth — basis for anti-monopoly legislation
State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy (1977): Split verdict on whether private resources count as 'material resources of the community'

UPSC trap: The question of whether privately owned resources constitute 'material resources of the community' under 39(b) remains judicially contested (Property Owners' Association v. State of Maharashtra — referred to larger bench)

concepts.name: Articles 14, 19 vs. DPSPs — Doctrine of 'Reasonable Restriction'
key_dimensions: Article 19 restrictions (clauses 2-6) include grounds like 'interests of general public' — courts read DPSPs into 'public interest' to uphold restrictions
Article 14 equality can be maintained while implementing DPSPs if intelligible differentia and rational nexus exist
State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951): DPSP-backed laws challenged under Article 19(1)(g) — court balanced both
UPSC trap: A DPSP alone cannot justify an Article 19 restriction — it must fit within the express grounds in Article 19(2)-(6)

concepts.name: Right to Health and Environmental DPSPs vs. Article 21
key_dimensions: Articles 47 (public health) and 48A (environment protection) as DPSPs expanded into Article 21's right to life
Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991): Right to pollution-free water and air is part of Article 21, drawing from Article 48A
MC Mehta series of cases: Environmental DPSPs (48A) used to expand and enforce environmental rights under Article 21
UPSC trap: Article 48A and Article 51A(g) (fundamental duty) together with Article 21 create a tripartite environmental protection framework

concepts.name: Article 21A vs. Article 15 — Reservation in Educational Institutions
key_dimensions: 93rd Amendment (2005) added Article 15(5): Enables reservation in private unaided educational institutions — classic DPSP accommodation into FR
PA Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005): SC held no reservation mandate on unaided private institutions → Parliament responded with 93rd Amendment
TMA Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002): Established a hierarchy — minority unaided > non-minority unaided > aided institutions in terms of state regulation
UPSC trap: Article 15(5) explicitly excludes minority educational institutions protected under Article 30 — a critical exception

concepts.name: Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) as a Bridge Between FRs and DPSPs
key_dimensions: 42nd Amendment (1976) added Part IVA (Article 51A) — Fundamental Duties link citizen obligations to DPSP objectives
Courts use Article 51A to interpret FRs restrictively where citizens violate duties (e.g., 51A(g) on environment)
AIIMS Students' Union v. AIIMS (2002): FDs are non-justiciable like DPSPs but can be used to assess reasonableness of restrictions on FRs
UPSC trap: FDs are in Part IVA, not Part IV — they are not DPSPs, but form the citizen-side complement to state-directed DPSPs

concepts.name: 42nd Amendment (1976) — The High-Water Mark of DPSP Supremacy
key_dimensions: Added Article 31D (anti-national activities — later repealed) and extended Article 31C to all DPSPs
Attempted to explicitly subordinate Articles 14, 19 to all DPSPs — reversed by Minerva Mills (1980)
Added 10 new DPSPs and Fundamental Duties — significantly expanded Part IV's scope
UPSC trap: The 42nd Amendment's attempt to make DPSPs superior to FRs was struck down — not the DPSPs themselves

concepts.name: Harmonious Construction: The Judicial Default Rule
key_dimensions: Courts prefer reading FRs and DPSPs together rather than treating them as conflicting — Pathumma v. State of Kerala (1978)
State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas (1976): Article 16(4) reservation for backward classes read harmoniously with Article 16(1) equality
Technique: DPSPs used to determine 'reasonableness' of restrictions on FRs — e.g., restriction is reasonable if it advances a DPSP goal
UPSC trap: Harmonious construction is the FIRST principle; conflict resolution (FR supremacy or Article 31C) is only invoked when harmony is impossible

concepts.name: Right to Property Evolution: Articles 19(1)(f) & 31 to Article 300A
key_dimensions: Pre-44th Amendment: Property was a FR under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 — the central battleground with DPSPs on land reform
44th Amendment (1978): Deleted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31; property became a legal right under Article 300A
Post-deletion: DPSPs on land/material resources face far less FR opposition; Article 300A only requires legal authority, not justification under Article 19 grounds
UPSC trap: Article 300A is in Part XII, not Part III — it is not a fundamental right and cannot be enforced via Article 32 (only via Article 226)
